title: Multiphysics Modeling of Thermo-Viscoelastic Damage in Functionally Graded Abradable Coatings with Probabilistic Geometric Tolerance Analysis
authors: Amjad El-Mellouhi, Yassine Adjal, Khaled Dhibi, Fedwa El-Mellouhi
abstract: In aircraft engines, functionally graded abradable coatings are used to control blade-tip clearance, but their durability is governed by effects that are often treated separately in existing models, including temperature-dependent viscoelastic softening, progressive damage, deposition-induced microstructural modulation, and geometric tolerances. This study integrates these effects within a unified multiphysics--probabilistic framework. The solved domain is a local through-thickness coating column driven by prescribed strain and temperature histories that include thermal eigenstrain and coating--substrate expansion mismatch. The results show that periodic property modulation increases end-of-cycle damage relative to the monotonic gradient and concentrates the maximum stress within a localized modulation crest. Propagating symmetric geometric tolerances through the coupled solver produces a strongly right-skewed damage distribution and a higher classification-level exceedance probability for the modulated gradient than for the monotonic gradient. This exceedance behavior cannot be obtained from a deterministic analysis performed at nominal geometry. The implementation is verified through spatial and temporal refinement, closed-form unit tests, nested Monte Carlo convergence with Wilson confidence intervals, and a hold-out-validated polynomial response surface. Numerical verification is clearly distinguished from experimental validation, and the simulated case is presented as a generic benchmark rather than an identified material model. The framework links deposition parameters and tolerance bands to damage-exceedance risk, supporting reliability-oriented screening of graded and multilayer coating systems.
summary: This paper presents a comprehensive multiphysics–probabilistic framework to model damage in advanced abradable coatings used in gas turbines. It uniquely integrates temperature-dependent viscoelasticity, progressive material damage, microstructural variations, and manufacturing geometric tolerances into one solver. The results highlight that considering these coupled uncertainties is critical for accurately assessing coating reliability.
main_problem: To develop a unified framework for predicting damage accumulation in functionally graded abradable coatings by integrating multiple, often separate, physical effects.
main_result: The study shows that combining periodic property modulation and geometric tolerances significantly increases the predicted end-of-cycle damage risk compared to analyzing these factors independently or deterministically.
method: A multiphysics–probabilistic framework is employed, coupling thermo-viscoelasticity, progressive damage laws, microstructural modulation, and Monte Carlo simulation for tolerance propagation.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a local through-thickness column of an abradable coating used in aircraft engines. The model incorporates temperature-dependent viscoelastic softening (Prony series) and stress-driven damage evolution.
key_observables: Damage variable (D), stress concentrations, damage-exceedance probability ($P_e$), and effective stiffness evolution.
important_parameters: Temperature history $T(z, t)$, applied strain $\epsilon_{app}(t)$, deposition modulation parameters, and geometric tolerance bands ($\delta u$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is a generic benchmark; it simplifies the problem by neglecting contact mechanics, wear depth prediction, and treating porosity via effective homogenization.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the block diagram of the multiphysics–probabilistic framework, showing the flow from input definitions through coupled solving to Monte Carlo sampling for outputs like exceedance probabilities.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for a unified model by identifying separate physical drivers (viscoelasticity, damage, modulation, tolerance). It details the coupling of these effects in the solver and presents results demonstrating how variability amplifies risk beyond deterministic predictions. The structure emphasizes verification procedures and limitations.
why_interesting: While highly applied to materials science, the rigorous implementation of nested Monte Carlo convergence with Wilson confidence intervals for quantifying uncertainty propagation in a complex coupled system is a sophisticated application of numerical methods relevant to reliability analysis in physics simulations.

A deter- ministic multiphysics core (property-field construction + coupled thermo-viscoelastic– damage solver) is wrapped by a probabilistic tolerance propagation layer (Monte Carlo sampling of geometric deviations) to produce both nominal predictions and reliability metrics.
